results.result: The manuscript challenges a key assumption in retinal ganglion cell (RGC) models by showing that anatomical and functional observations indicate surrounds are added before the summation of signals across receptive field subunits that creates the center, rather than only to the fully formed center signal.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 establish the context and motivation for the study. C1 is well-established knowledge, C2 accurately describes existing models (supported by citations C9), and C3 is supported by anatomical and functional studies (C10-C12). These claims provide a solid foundation for the study's hypothesis.

results.result: The surround can control sensitivity to fine spatial structure by changing how the center integrates visual information over space, particularly when center and surround signals are correlated as in natural stimuli.
results.evaluation: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches (Figures 2-3, natural images and gratings). Claims C21, C32, C42, C74, and C98 all converge on this conclusion from different experimental paradigms. The effect is particularly prominent with correlated center-surround signals (C5), which is demonstrated experimentally.

results.result: Off parasol RGCs show maximal spatial contrast sensitivity when center and surround experience similar mean luminance, with bright surrounds reducing nonlinear sensitivity and dark surrounds suppressing responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C29 and C43 are directly supported by experimental data in Figure 2 using natural images. The systematic relationship between center-surround luminance difference and spatial contrast sensitivity is clearly demonstrated across multiple cells and stimuli.

results.result: Split-field grating experiments confirm that surround modulation of spatial integration is maximal when center and surround experience the same mean luminance, and this effect is present in bipolar synaptic output rather than post-synaptic mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C38 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3. The similarity between excitatory inputs and spike responses (C37) supports the inference that the effect originates in bipolar synaptic output (C38). The grating experiments provide converging evidence with the natural image experiments.

results.result: Similar center-surround interactions occur in On parasol RGCs, though they are more easily shifted into linear spatial integration compared to Off parasol RGCs, suggesting this is a general feature of center-surround RF organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 and C123 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and throughout the manuscript. The difference between On and Off cells is consistent with prior work (C22, C41) showing shallower rectification in On cells.

results.result: Computational modeling using linear-nonlinear cascades demonstrates that center and surround signals combine linearly before passing through a shared nonlinearity, rather than through independent nonlinearities.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47 are supported by quantitative model comparison in Figure 4. The shared model outperforms the independent model and performs as well as the more complex stacked model despite having fewer parameters. Claims C54-C55 show that model predictions match experimental observations.

results.result: The relationship between center activation and excitatory conductance depends on surround activation, with rectification decreasing as the surround becomes more depolarizing, and Off cells showing stronger rectification than On cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C53 are directly supported by experimental data in Figure 5. The systematic relationship between surround activation and center rectification is clearly demonstrated, and the difference between On and Off cells is consistent with prior work (C53).

results.result: Natural movie stimuli elicit sublinear interactions between center and surround that are present in excitatory synaptic inputs and largely inherited by spike outputs, demonstrating that nonlinear center-surround interactions are prominent for naturalistic visual inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C63 and C65 are supported by experimental data in Figure 6 using naturalistic movie stimuli. The correlation between excitatory inputs and spike outputs (C61-C62) supports the inference that spike nonlinearities inherit properties from synaptic inputs. The difference between On and Off cells (C63) is consistent with known differences in inhibitory input (C64).

results.result: Nonlinear center-surround interactions depend strongly on center-surround intensity correlations, with sublinear interactions becoming more prominent as correlations increase from negative to positive values.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C73 and C75 are supported by experimental data in Figure 7. The systematic manipulation of center-surround correlations (natural, shuffled, and controlled noise stimuli) provides strong evidence for the dependence of nonlinear interactions on spatial correlations.

results.result: Luminance-matched surround activation decreases the sensitivity of nonlinear spatial integration to changes in mean luminance, with spatial contrast sensitivity being restored when dark gratings are paired with luminance-matched surrounds.
results.evaluation: Claims C76 and C79-C84 are supported by experimental data in Figure 8B-C using modified grating stimuli. The systematic relationship between surround matching and spatial contrast sensitivity across different center luminances is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Natural images provide inputs to the surround that preserve spatial contrast sensitivity of the RF center compared to center inputs alone, with sensitivity being 2-3 times greater with matched surrounds, due to the ability of the surround to control bipolar subunit rectification and the positive correlations in natural images.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C92 are supported by experimental data in Figure 8D-F using natural image patches. The comparison between matched, shuffled, and no surround conditions provides strong evidence for the role of natural spatial correlations in preserving spatial contrast sensitivity. The quantitative enhancement (2-3 fold, C89) is directly measured.

results.result: Computational modeling with nonlinear subunits shows that stronger RF surrounds are associated with greater spatial contrast sensitivity, especially for images with strong local luminance signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C97 are supported by computational modeling results in Figure 8G-I. The model predictions are consistent with experimental observations and provide mechanistic insight into how surround strength affects spatial contrast sensitivity.

results.result: The incorporation of an antagonistic surround before formation of the nonlinear center mitigates the effect of mean intensity changes on spatial contrast sensitivity for natural scenes, extending the classical role of the surround in reducing sensitivity to mean luminance changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C106 synthesize the experimental findings into a coherent mechanistic explanation. These claims are supported by the convergence of evidence from multiple experimental approaches and are consistent with known properties of natural vision (C99) and surround function (C103).

results.result: Capturing RGC center-surround interactions and spatial contrast sensitivity requires incorporating the impact of the surround on subunits within the receptive field center, consistent with observations that surrounds are present in diffuse bipolar cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C110 are supported by the experimental findings and modeling results throughout the manuscript. The conclusion that RF models need to incorporate surround effects on subunits (C110) follows logically from the demonstrated importance of this architecture (C108) and is consistent with anatomical observations (C109).

results.result: Natural scenes contain strong spatial correlations, and while the RF surround can decorrelate population responses, recent findings show that other mechanisms like nonlinear processing and fixational eye movements may play larger roles.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C8 accurately summarize prior work on natural scene statistics and surround function. These are well-supported by the cited literature and provide important context for the study's findings about surround function in natural vision.

results.result: Classical and modern RF models assume the surround interacts only with the fully formed center signal, but anatomically, surrounds are generated by horizontal and amacrine cells and are present in bipolar cells, where the degree of synaptic rectification can control spatial integration properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C14 accurately describe the state of the field and the anatomical basis for the study's hypothesis. These claims are well-supported by extensive citations to prior work and provide the foundation for the study's novel contribution.

results.result: Synaptic rectification at the bipolar-to-RGC synapse controls spatial integration properties, with linear synapses yielding linear integration and rectified synapses yielding nonlinear integration that causes strong responses to gratings and natural images, particularly in Off parasol RGCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C20 accurately describe prior work on spatial integration in parasol RGCs. These claims are well-supported by citations and provide essential background for understanding the study's findings. The focus on Off parasol RGCs (C20) is justified by prior work.

results.result: Off parasol RGCs show stronger rectification and nonlinear spatial integration than On parasol cells, with nonlinear integration endowing sensitivity to spatial contrast in natural images.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C24 accurately describe prior work that motivates the focus on Off parasol RGCs. These claims are supported by appropriate citations and provide justification for the experimental design.

results.result: Surround hyperpolarization of bipolar cells shifts synapses into a quiescent state diminishing responses, while surround depolarization reduces nonlinear sensitivity of the center.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31 are mechanistic interpretations supported by the experimental data and knowledge of synaptic function. These interpretations are consistent with the observed effects of bright and dark surrounds on spatial contrast sensitivity.

results.result: Naturalistic center and surround stimuli tend to elicit responses at different times, consistent with spatial correlations in natural images and the antagonistic nature of the surround.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67 are supported by experimental observations in Figure 6 and are consistent with known properties of natural images and surround function. This observation helps explain why nonlinear interactions are prominent in natural vision.

results.result: Decreased mean luminance over the RF center depolarizes bipolar synapses shifting them into a locally linear state and decreasing spatial contrast sensitivity, but a luminance-matched surround can partially cancel this depolarization and preserve sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 are mechanistic predictions based on knowledge of synaptic function that are tested and supported by the experimental data in Figure 8. These claims provide a clear mechanistic framework for understanding the experimental results.

results.result: The nonlinearity index is lower for randomly selected images than for grating stimuli because grating spatial structure is designed to differentially activate subunits while random image patches often lack such structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C95 are supported by comparison of experimental data in Figure 8 and are consistent with knowledge of how different stimuli interact with RF structure. This observation helps interpret the differences between grating and natural image experiments.

results.result: The nonlinear relationship between bipolar cell input and RGC excitatory input is assumed to arise at the bipolar-to-RGC synapse based on prior work, though contributions from earlier nonlinearities in bipolar cells are likely, such as active conductances in bipolar cell axons.
results.evaluation: Claim C111 is explicitly stated as an assumption based on prior work in mouse retina, which may not fully apply to primate retina. Claims C112-C113 are speculative statements about possible additional mechanisms. While these are reasonable interpretations, they are not directly tested in this study.

results.result: RGC RF surrounds can show nonlinear spatial integration, and if this substantially shapes surround suppression, then spatial structure of the surround should contribute to center-surround interactions, leading to predictions about enhanced spatial contrast sensitivity with appropriately structured surrounds.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C119 discuss nonlinear spatial integration in the surround, which is supported by prior work (C114, C116) but is not directly investigated in this study. Claims C115, C117, and C119 are speculative statements about future research directions. While these are interesting predictions, they are not tested here.

results.result: The LN cascade models used do not capture all relevant mechanisms shaping RGC excitatory input, such as history-dependent mechanisms like contrast and luminance adaptation, though other work has explored more sophisticated models.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C122 are appropriate acknowledgments of model limitations supported by citations to relevant literature. This is important context for interpreting the modeling results and does not undermine the main conclusions.

results.result: Any RGC with rectified bipolar subunits with surrounds should show similar center-surround interactions at the level of excitatory inputs, though direct inhibitory inputs could further shape these interactions, particularly in On parasol RGCs where inhibition strongly shapes natural image responses.
results.evaluation: Claim C124 is a reasonable generalization from the experimental findings. Claims C125-C126 acknowledge the potential role of inhibition, which is supported by experimental data (Figure 6) and prior work. These claims appropriately qualify the generality of the findings.

results.result: Similar RF subregion interactions are present in other visual neurons such as V1, where suppressive subunits can change the nonlinear relationship between excitatory subunit activation and spike response, and surrounds are strongest in homogeneous contexts, similar to the contextual effects observed in retinal surrounds with luminance correlations.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C131 draw appropriate parallels between the findings in retina and prior work in V1. These comparisons are supported by citations and help place the findings in a broader context of visual processing. The parallel to V1 contextual effects (C129-C131) is particularly insightful.

results.result: The circuit mechanisms underlying the observed center-surround interactions—nonlinear synaptic transfer functions and convergence of parallel pathways—are ubiquitous in neural circuits, with convergence prior to nonlinear elements allowing one circuit to regulate the effective nonlinearity applied to signals in another circuit.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C134 are well-supported generalizations from the experimental findings. Claim C135 is speculative about possible circuit mechanisms but is grounded in known circuit motifs. These claims appropriately place the findings in a broader neuroscience context.

results.result: Complex neural computations need not rely on exotic circuitry; interactions of known circuit elements can produce diverse computations under different stimulus conditions by modulating the impact of nonlinear mechanisms, highlighting the importance of exploring circuit mechanisms under diverse and naturalistic stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C138 are appropriate general conclusions from the study's findings. These claims emphasize the importance of studying neural circuits under naturalistic conditions and are well-supported by the experimental results showing context-dependent changes in spatial integration.

results.result: Inhibitory input impacts On parasol responses to natural stimuli more than Off parasol responses.
results.evaluation: Claim C64 is supported by citation to prior work and is consistent with the experimental observations in Figure 6 showing weaker correlation between excitatory inputs and spike outputs in On cells. This helps explain differences between On and Off parasol RGCs.
